Alexander Cole's Testimony in support
of LD 1035
Good morning Senator Tepler and Representative Doudera and honorable members of the environment and natural resources committee.
My name is Alexander Cole. l proposed the concept for this bill to Representative Rana.
l am an engineer at the University of Maine, a lifelong Mainer, and an outdoor enthusiast.
l use a fair amount of propane when l'm camping or fishing, either to stay warm or to cook food on a camping stove. After a few years, those little camping gas canisters started piling up in my garage: you know, the tiny green Coleman ones. l started wondering, how do I get rid of these?
Thus began the propane tank rabbit hole.
You'd likely recognize a 20lb propane tank: it's the white-colored tank you would normally use for a household grill- those are rated to be refilled, and reusable; you can swap used ones for
'
new ones at basically any gas station. There's a system for them.
But the tiny green ones are a different story, because while these "camping gas" tanks might be
painted green, there's nothing "green" about them. To my discovery, there is virtually no
mechanism for disposing of these tanks; tanks with highly explosive gas. These tanks are sold in 12 packs at Walmart, and are designed to be single-use. Disposable.
There's little to no guidance on where to put them. The closest hazardous waste disposal site to Bangor, which is in Lewiston, won't accept them unless you puncture them first, which is already dangerous. You can't legally refill them. The absolute best case scenario is that these little cans end up in a landfill. Considering that an estimated 60 million of these are sold in the United States each year, l think it's worth asking: where are they all going?
This issue has bothered me for a long time. l'd personally argue that we should ban the sale of single-use propane tanks altogether, but l recognize that we need to start somewhere. And the
study proposed by this bill is certainly a goodstart.
Thank you.

Testimony ofRepresentative Ambureen Rana introducing
LD 1035, Resolve, to Study the Safe Disposal of Single-use Propane Canisters
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Environment and Natural Resources
Good morning, Senator Tepler, Representative Doudera and distinguished members of the
Environment and Natural Resources Committee. My name is Ambureen Rana, and I have the
honor of representing House District 21, which includes part of the City of Bangor.

I am here today to introduce LD 1035, Resolve, to Study the Safe Disposal of Single-use
Propane Canisters.

This measure directs the Department of Enviromnental Protection to study the current
infrastructure for the disposal of single-use propane canisters and make recommendations regarding improvements around disposing them safely, which is to be detailed in a report given
to this committee in December. Further, LD 1035 directs the department to evaluate how
single-use propane canisters may be managed as part of the Stewardship Program for Packaging.
Currently, it's a real challenge to safely get rid of propane canisters.
_
In my community, some metal recycling centers like AIM Recycling will only accept propane
canisters if they have a hole punched in them or they're out in half -- something that isn't possible for some community members to do either because they don't have the tools to do it, don't feel safe doing it, or both.
Stories of propane canisters exploding are not uncommon, and without a collection program in place, these canisters just stick around people's homes posing a hazard, or even worse, get dumped in places where they shouldn't be like our lakes, rivers and ponds or in the woods.
I believe that LD 1035 is necessary so that we can begin to learn how to manage the disposal of
these canisters more properly. Thank you for your time. I am happy to answer any questions you may have.

L.D. 1035, as printed, would require the Department to conduct a study and make recommendations to the legislature by December 3, 2025, regarding the current infrastructure for disposal of single-use propane canisters. The bill requires that the
Department evaluate the viability of establishing a ban on the disposal of these items.

The Department already has the authority to evaluate whether single-use propane canisters meet the criteria to be a candidate for a product stewardship program under 38 M.R.S. � 1772(2). In addition, single-use propane canisters also meet the definition of packaging under 38 l\/l.R.S. � 2146, Maine's Stewardship Program for Packaging, and therefore will be included in the program's implementation in 2027. Because there are already pathways to manage single-use propane canisters in Maine law via stewardship programs, the Department does not see any reason to evaluate a ban of these items. implementing and enforcing a ban will not necessarily make it any easier
for consumers to dispose of these common items, and therefore they may be more effectively managed through product stewardship.

Under the Stewardship Program for Packaging, producers sending single-use propane canisters into the state will be required to report their sales of this packaging material and pay a fee based on the cost of handling this material and the amount each producer of these canisters sends into the State. This program also provides an opportunity for producers of packaging to establish an alternative collection program to collect and
manage their packaging. Producers of these canisters could therefore elect to stand up their own alternative collection program through the Stewardship Program for Packaging and avoid paying some of the fees that they would owe to the program.

Instead of a stand-alone study, the Department would support an amendment of LD
1035 to require the Department to evaluate the disposal of single use propane cylinders as part of the stewardship program annual report under 38 M.R.S. � 1772(1), due to the legislature by February 15, 2026. As part of the evaluation, the Department will provide

Testimony of Sarah Woodbuiy, Vice President of Policy and Advocacy, Defend Our Health In Support of LD 1035, "Resolve, to Study the Safe Disposal of Single-use Propane Canisters"
Before the Environment and Natural Resources Committee March 24, 2025
Senator Tepler, Representative Doudera, and members of the Environment and Natural
Resources Committee. My name is Sarah Woodbury. I am the Vice President of Policy and
Advocacy for Defend Our Health. Defend Our Health's mission is to make sure that everyone
has equal access to safe food and drinking water, healthy homes, and products that are toxic-
free and climate friendly. l am here to testify in support of LD 1035, "Resolve, to Study the Safe
Disposal of Single-use Propane Canisters" .
Single-use propane tanks are an easy, affordable way for popular people that camp or are
hosting cookouts to be able to cook meals outdoors. Unforunately, the state of Maine doesn't
have a good system set up for people to be able to dispose of these canisters, with some people having to drive several hours to a facility to take them. This isn't a viable way to manage
the collection of these canisters, particularly in a state as large and rural as Maine. This leads to people either having a large collection of them -in their homes, being left behind as litter at campsites, or inproperly disposing of them in landfills or other facilities. This is dangerous. lf the
canisters still have any of the fuel in them, they could explode. This was the case in January of 2020 when a propane canister exploded at the Hampden waste facility causing a fire and injuring a worker. lt also caused the facility to have to shut down while the assessed the damage` .
Propane canisters should be managed under Maine's Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) law. lt's our understanding that Rep. Rana has an amendment to to her original bill that will
require the DEP to evaluate if they meet the criteria for the EPR law and how they should be managed. Disposing of these canisters can be dangerous and we need to have an appropriate
program set up so folks can dispose of them safely. We support Rep. Rana's amendment and
urge the committee to vote "ought to pass as amended" on LD 1035.

Testimony in Support of
LD 1035, Resolve, to Study the Safe Disposal of Single-use Propane Canisters
Vanessa Berry, NRCM Sustainable Maine Program Manager
March 24, 2025
Senator Tepler, Representative Doudera, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on
Environment and Natural Resources, my name is Vanessa Berry. I am the Sustainable Maine
Program Manager for the Natural Resources Council of Maine (NRCM). I appreciate this
opportunity to testify in support of LD 1035.
NRCM is Maine's leading environmental advocacy organization. Our staff, members, and
supporters are avid supporters of outdoor recreation. Because of this, we support initiatives to make outdoor recreation experiences more sustainable.
One-pound propane cylinders are used for lanterns, cooking appliances, portable heaters, and other outdoor gear. The design of these canisters makes them very useful for travel, but canister disposal is problematic. The valves used to fill these small propane canisters are not designed to be refilled.
This makes it difficult to know whether containers are fully emptied, making the vessels single use by design and posing safety risks when handling the empty containers. Several years ago, I personally experienced a near-miss during a dangerous incident in a recycling facility when a propane canister was compacted with other ferrous metals in a baler. These small tanks contain a
lot of pressure and pose serious risks to waste haulers, transfer station operators, and material
processors who might encounter them unknowingly if they're discarded in a trash bag or mixed in
a large pile of residential recycling.
Currently there are very few options for proper disposal or recycling of these one-pound cylinders,
which results in improper and unsafe disposal or littering of these containers. However, as we
understand it, one-pound propane cylinders should be covered within Maine's Product Stewardship Program for Packaging, which is in its early stages of implementation. With fees on packaging based on their recyclability and other factors, this program should encourage manufacturers to consider alternative design for their packaging to allow the containers to be safely refilled by consumers or otherwise incentivize the use of an alternative collection program, such as an exchange of containers similar to retail programs existing for 20-pound propane tanks.
LD 1035 recognizes that single-use propane tanks can pose safety challenges in the waste stream
and may warrant their own take-back system to provide for safe, responsible collection for used
propane cylinders at the end of their useful life. We support the proposed evaluation of the current infrastructure for such a collection program, as proposed by LD 1035, and to also explore possible
restrictions on propane tanks that are not designed to be refillable. I appreciate the opportunity to
share these thoughts on LD 1035.

Testimony in support of LD 1035: Resolve, to Study the Safe Disposal of Single-use Propane Canisters
Victor Horton, Executive Director, Maine Resource Recovery Association March 24, 2025
Senator Tepler, Representative Doudera, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Environment and Natural Resources, my name is Victor Horton. I am the Executive Director of the Maine Resource Recovery Association (MRRA). I appreciate the opportunity to testify in support of LD 1035.
The Maine Resource Recovery Association ("MRRA") is a nonprofit organization committed to supporting professional and sustainable materials management in Maine. Established in 1984, MRRA serves over 160 municipalities through its work to provide ongoing education on waste regulations, evolving waste streams, and best practices. We also assist in operating 60 transfer stations and recycling centers and help members find markets for recyclable materials, reinforcing Maine's commitment to resource recovery.
LD 1035 would afford an opportunity to study and take a closer look at a take back program or a deposit system to get the one pound propane tanks recycled and out of the waste stream.
Adding these canisters to the Extended Producer Responsibility Law seems like a good approach.
Currently there is no statewide program to collect, recycle, or dispose of these one pound canisters.
The one pound propane tanks can be found for sale in retail outlets that sell grocery, camping supplies, hardware, and convenience stores and possibly many other department stores.
I have recently spoken with several of our member towns and metal recyclers in the hopes of getting a better understanding of their handling of these items.
I found that the recycling methods are inconsistent state-wide.
Some towns have a vendor that collects them at their facility for a fee and a NH company hauls them off.

Another sends them to Ohio in bulk for recycling at a higher cost to recycle than the purchase price.
Several scrap metal vendors do not accept them at all while others will take them mixed with scrap metal and still others require them to be brought in separated from metal.
With regards to safety: these tanks are fairly small so sometimes they may slip through the steel can recycling stream and inadvertently be baled with scrap cans by a town employee. This could cause an explosion as some of the tanks come in with residual propane still in them.
When no easily accessible recycling outlet is available, they seem to become litter and end up in our woods and wild lands.
Having one pound propane tanks as part of EPR would send a consistent message to residents that there are reliable safe ways to dispose of them.
For these reasons, we urge the Committee to support LD 1035.
Victor Horton
